result.summary: Phaëton is buried by the Naiads, and his father hides his face in grief while his mother Clymene searches the earth for his bones. His sisters mourn at the tomb until they turn into poplars, and their tears harden into amber.

scenes.title: Burial of Phaëton
scenes.summary: The Naiads bury Phaëton and carve an epitaph. The Sun hides his face, and a day passes without sunlight.

scenes.title: Clymene finds the bones
scenes.summary: Clymene wanders the earth in grief, finds her son's bones and lies weeping on his tomb.
scenes.stakes: She has lost her son and can only mourn him.

scenes.title: Sisters become poplars
scenes.summary: The Heliades mourn at the tomb for four months, then turn into trees as Clymene tries to save them. Their tears harden into amber.
scenes.stakes: The sisters lose their human bodies and their mother loses them as well.

alias_notes.explanation: The Heliades are named by their father, the Sun (Helios).

notable_quotes.reason: Phaëton's famous epitaph praising a great attempt despite failure.
A daughter's last pleading words as the bark closes over her.

analysis.text: Grief and metamorphosis: mourning freezes the sisters into trees, and their tears become a lasting natural object, amber.
The passage gives a mythical origin for amber, which Romans prized as jewelry and imported from the Baltic region.

legacy.text: The Heliades turning into poplars and weeping amber became a favored image in later European art and poetry.

fun_facts.text: Amber is fossilized tree resin, so Ovid's story of tears hardening into amber echoes its real origin.

language_notes.text: Hesperian Naiads: water nymphs of the western land (Hesperia, Italy or the west), where Phaëton fell into the river Eridanus. Naiads are nymphs of rivers and springs.
"Three-forked flames" means Jove's triple thunderbolt, which struck Phaëton from the chariot.
The "advantage" is wry: the world still had light from the fires Phaëton's disaster started.
The Moon filling her disk four times means four months have passed.
Latian: of Latium, the region around Rome. Roman women are meant.

context_notes.text: Clymene is Phaëton's mother, a mortal whose son claimed the Sun as father, which led to his fatal drive.
The daughters of the Sun are the Heliades, Phaëton's sisters, named here as Phaëthusa and Lampetie.
Amber is fossilized tree resin. The myth explains its origin as hardened tears of the Heliades, carried by the river Eridanus.

literary_notes.text: The inscription sums up Phaëton's story in a compact verse, praising his daring while admitting his failure.
A whole day without the sun conveys the god's grief in cosmic terms; the narrator distances himself with "if we can believe it."
Clymene warming the cold carved name with her breast makes her grief physical and tender.
The slow creeping of bark upward, leaving only the mouths free, makes the transformation gradual and horrifying.
Blood flowing from the torn branches shows the sisters are still human beneath the bark, and heightens the mother's helpless anguish.
The plain statement that bark covered their last words ends the sisters' speech abruptly and quietly.
